claim: The neonatal mouse cerebellum shows remarkable regenerative potential upon injury at birth.
source: The neonatal mouse cerebellum shows remarkable regenerative potential upon injury at birth, wherein a subset of Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) undergoes adaptive reprogramming to replenish granule cell progenitors that die.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Wojcinski et al., 2017, Bayin et al., 2021, Bayin et al., 2018; Altman and Anderson, 1971).

claim: A subset of Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) undergoes adaptive reprogramming to replenish granule cell progenitors that die upon injury at birth.
source: The neonatal mouse cerebellum shows remarkable regenerative potential upon injury at birth, wherein a subset of Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) undergoes adaptive reprogramming to replenish granule cell progenitors that die.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic and bulk chromatin accessibility analyses of NEPs from injured neonatal cerebella show a temporary increase in cellular processes involved in responding to reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Single-cell transcriptomic and bulk chromatin accessibility analyses of the NEPs from injured neonatal cerebella compared to controls show a temporary increase in cellular processes involved in responding to reactive oxygen species (ROS), a known damage-associated molecular pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq and ATAC-seq data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: ROS is a known damage-associated molecular pattern.
source: Single-cell transcriptomic and bulk chromatin accessibility analyses of the NEPs from injured neonatal cerebella compared to controls show a temporary increase in cellular processes involved in responding to reactive oxygen species (ROS), a known damage-associated molecular pattern.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Analysis of ROS levels in cerebellar tissue confirms a transient increase 1 day after injury at postnatal day 1.
source: Analysis of ROS levels in cerebellar tissue confirms a transient increase 1 day after injury at postnatal day 1, overlapping with the peak cell death in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The transient increase in ROS 1 day after injury overlaps with the peak cell death in the cerebellum.
source: Analysis of ROS levels in cerebellar tissue confirms a transient increase 1 day after injury at postnatal day 1, overlapping with the peak cell death in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In a transgenic mouse line that ubiquitously overexpresses human mitochondrial catalase (mCAT), ROS is reduced 1 day after injury to the granule cell progenitors.
source: In a transgenic mouse line that ubiquitously overexpresses human mitochondrial catalase (mCAT), ROS is reduced 1 day after injury to the granule cell progenitors, and we demonstrate that several steps in the regenerative process of NEPs are curtailed, leading to reduced cerebellar growth.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: Several steps in the regenerative process of NEPs are curtailed in mCAT mice, leading to reduced cerebellar growth.
source: In a transgenic mouse line that ubiquitously overexpresses human mitochondrial catalase (mCAT), ROS is reduced 1 day after injury to the granule cell progenitors, and we demonstrate that several steps in the regenerative process of NEPs are curtailed, leading to reduced cerebellar growth.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing reduced EGL replenishment and cerebellar size.

claim: Microglia are involved in one step of adaptive reprogramming by regulating NEP replenishment of the granule cell precursors.
source: We also provide preliminary evidence that microglia are involved in one step of adaptive reprogramming by regulating NEP replenishment of the granule cell precursors.
evidence: This is supported by PLX5622 treatment experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Changes in the tissue microenvironment regulate multiple steps in adaptive reprogramming of NEPs upon death of cerebellar granule cell progenitors at birth.
source: Collectively, our results highlight that changes in the tissue microenvironment regulate multiple steps in adaptive reprogramming of NEPs upon death of cerebellar granule cell progenitors at birth, highlighting the instructive roles of microenvironmental signals during regeneration of the neonatal brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The microenvironment surrounding a brain injury and the cellular responses elicited in the remaining cells are key determinants of how efficiently a repair process will unfold.
source: The microenvironment surrounding a brain injury and the cellular responses elicited in the remaining cells are key determinants of how efficiently a repair process will unfold.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014).

claim: An important factor underlying the effectiveness of regenerative responses to an injury is the plasticity of the stem/progenitor cells in a tissue.
source: An important factor underlying the effectiveness of regenerative responses to an injury is the plasticity of the stem/progenitor cells in a tissue (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The neonatal mouse cerebellum has a remarkable capacity to regenerate cells ablated around birth.
source: The neonatal mouse cerebellum has a remarkable capacity to regenerate cells ablated around birth (Wojcinski et al., 2017, Bayin et al., 2021, Bayin et al., 2018; Altman and Anderson, 1971).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The cerebellum provides an ideal system to study the roles that signals in the microenvironment play in key steps of the repair process in the brain.
source: Thus, the cerebellum provides an ideal system to study the roles that signals in the microenvironment play in key steps of the repair process in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the regenerative capacity of the neonatal cerebellum.

claim: The cerebellum is a folded hindbrain structure that is critical for motor coordination.
source: The cerebellum is a folded hindbrain structure that is critical for motor coordination.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge.

claim: The cerebellum participates in higher-order social and cognitive behaviors through its circuit connections with all other brain regions.
source: It also participates in higher-order social and cognitive behaviors through its circuit connections with all other brain regions (Badura et al., 2018; Buckner, 2013; Burda and Sofroniew, 2014; Salman and Tsai, 2016; Strick et al., 2009; Tomlinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Compared to the rest of the brain, the cerebellum has protracted development, as its major growth occurs during the first 2 weeks after birth in mice.
source: Compared to the rest of the brain, the cerebellum has protracted development, as its major growth occurs during the first 2 weeks after birth in mice and at least 6 months surrounding birth in humans (Altman and Bayer, 1997; Rakic and Sidman, 1970; Dobbing and Sands, 1973).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The major growth of the cerebellum occurs at least 6 months surrounding birth in humans.
source: Compared to the rest of the brain, the cerebellum has protracted development, as its major growth occurs during the first 2 weeks after birth in mice and at least 6 months surrounding birth in humans (Altman and Bayer, 1997; Rakic and Sidman, 1970; Dobbing and Sands, 1973).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The timing of the major growth of the cerebellum makes it susceptible to injury around birth.
source: This timing of the major growth of the cerebellum makes it susceptible to injury around birth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental timeline.

claim: Cerebellar hypoplasia is the second leading risk factor for autism spectrum disorders.
source: Indeed, cerebellar hypoplasia is the second leading risk factor for autism spectrum disorders, and cerebellar injury around birth can have devastating outcomes and significant effects on subsequent quality of life (Tsai et al., 2018; Stoodley et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cerebellar injury around birth can have devastating outcomes and significant effects on subsequent quality of life.
source: Indeed, cerebellar hypoplasia is the second leading risk factor for autism spectrum disorders, and cerebellar injury around birth can have devastating outcomes and significant effects on subsequent quality of life (Tsai et al., 2018; Stoodley et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All the cell types in the cerebellum are derived from two progenitor zones, the embryonic rhombic lip and the ventricular zone.
source: All the cell types in the cerebellum are derived from two progenitor zones, the embryonic rhombic lip and the ventricular zone that give rise to the excitatory neurons, or the inhibitory neurons and glia, respectively (Leto et al., 2016; Joyner and Bayin, 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The rhombic lip gives rise to excitatory neurons.
source: All the cell types in the cerebellum are derived from two progenitor zones, the embryonic rhombic lip and the ventricular zone that give rise to the excitatory neurons, or the inhibitory neurons and glia, respectively (Leto et al., 2016; Joyner and Bayin, 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ventricular zone gives rise to inhibitory neurons and glia.
source: All the cell types in the cerebellum are derived from two progenitor zones, the embryonic rhombic lip and the ventricular zone that give rise to the excitatory neurons, or the inhibitory neurons and glia, respectively (Leto et al., 2016; Joyner and Bayin, 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During postnatal growth, the rhombic lip-derived granule cell precursors (GCPs) cover the surface of the cerebellum in a structure named the external granule layer (EGL).
source: During postnatal growth, the rhombic lip-derived granule cell precursors (GCPs) cover the surface of the cerebellum in a structure named the external granule layer (EGL) and continue to proliferate in a sonic hedgehog (SHH) dependent manner for 2 weeks after birth in mice (Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; McMahon et al., 2003; Corrales et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GCPs continue to proliferate in a sonic hedgehog (SHH) dependent manner for 2 weeks after birth in mice.
source: During postnatal growth, the rhombic lip-derived granule cell precursors (GCPs) cover the surface of the cerebellum in a structure named the external granule layer (EGL) and continue to proliferate in a sonic hedgehog (SHH) dependent manner for 2 weeks after birth in mice (Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; McMahon et al., 2003; Corrales et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Following their exit from the cell cycle, the granule cells (GCs) migrate inward to form the internal granule layer (IGL).
source: Following their exit from the cell cycle, the granule cells (GCs) migrate inward to form the internal granule layer (IGL).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Gliogenic Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) express SOX2 and generate astroglia (astrocytes and Bergman glia).
source: Other SHH-dependent progenitor populations of the neonatal cerebellum are either gliogenic Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) that express SOX2 and generate astroglia (astrocytes and Bergman glia) or neurogenic-NEPs that generate late-born interneurons (Bayin et al., 2021, Cerrato et al., 2018; Parmigiani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurogenic-NEPs generate late-born interneurons.
source: Other SHH-dependent progenitor populations of the neonatal cerebellum are either gliogenic Nestin-expressing progenitors (NEPs) that express SOX2 and generate astroglia (astrocytes and Bergman glia) or neurogenic-NEPs that generate late-born interneurons (Bayin et al., 2021, Cerrato et al., 2018; Parmigiani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gliogenic-NEPs reside either in the Bergmann glia layer (BgL) intermixed with Purkinje cells and generate Bergmann glia (Bg) and astrocytes, or in the white matter (WM) in the center of the lobules and generate astrocytes.
source: Gliogenic-NEPs reside either in the Bergmann glia layer (BgL) intermixed with Purkinje cells and generate Bergmann glia (Bg) and astrocytes, or in the white matter (WM) in the center of the lobules (folds) and generate astrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NEP localization and fate.

claim: Neurogenic-NEPs are restricted to the WM and produce interneurons that migrate outward to the outermost molecular layer.
source: Neurogenic-NEPs are restricted to the WM and produce interneurons that migrate outward to the outermost molecular layer (Bayin et al., 2021, Brown et al., 2020; De Luca et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When the GCPs are killed upon injury soon after birth, the gliogenic-NEPs in the BgL (BgL-NEPs) undergo adaptive reprogramming to generate GCPs and replenish the EGL.
source: Surprisingly, when the GCPs are killed upon injury soon after birth, the gliogenic-NEPs in the BgL (BgL-NEPs) undergo adaptive reprogramming to generate GCPs and replenish the EGL via a transitory cellular state that involves upregulation of the neurogenic gene Ascl1 to promote a glial-to-neural fate switch (Wojcinski et al., 2017, Bayin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Adaptive reprogramming involves a transitory cellular state that involves upregulation of the neurogenic gene Ascl1 to promote a glial-to-neural fate switch.
source: Surprisingly, when the GCPs are killed upon injury soon after birth, the gliogenic-NEPs in the BgL (BgL-NEPs) undergo adaptive reprogramming to generate GCPs and replenish the EGL via a transitory cellular state that involves upregulation of the neurogenic gene Ascl1 to promote a glial-to-neural fate switch (Wojcinski et al., 2017, Bayin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Adaptive reprogramming involves multiple sequential stages starting with increased proliferation of BgL-NEPs, then a fate switch to neuronal progenitors, migration to the site of injury (EGL), and acquisition of a GCP identity.
source: Adaptive reprogramming involves multiple sequential stages starting with increased proliferation of BgL-NEPs, then a fate switch to neuronal progenitors, migration to the site of injury (EGL), and acquisition of a GCP identity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the adaptive reprogramming process.

claim: In the adult brain, numerous cell types communicate and provide a concerted response to injury, including astrocytes, microglia (macrophages of the brain), and stem cells of the neurogenic niches.
source: In the adult brain, numerous cell types communicate and provide a concerted response to injury, including astrocytes, microglia (macrophages of the brain), and stem cells of the neurogenic niches (Frik et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Upon traumatic brain injury, cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), which act as an inflammatory stimulus and activate microglia that can lead to gliosis, eventually causing neurotoxicity and scarring.
source: For example, upon traumatic brain injury, cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), which act as an inflammatory stimulus and activate microglia that can lead to gliosis, eventually causing neurotoxicity and scarring (Donat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cellular composition and microenvironment of the early postnatal brain are very different from the adult.
source: However, the cellular composition and microenvironment of the early postnatal brain are very different from the adult.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the neonatal cerebellum, microglia are immature and are still being generated.
source: In the neonatal cerebellum, microglia are immature (Li et al., 2019) and are still being generated, and NEPs and GCPs are actively proliferating and producing astroglia and neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the neonatal cerebellum, NEPs and GCPs are actively proliferating and producing astroglia and neurons.
source: In the neonatal cerebellum, microglia are immature (Li et al., 2019) and are still being generated, and NEPs and GCPs are actively proliferating and producing astroglia and neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the spinal cord, while neonatal microglia and astrocytes facilitate scarless repair, the same cells in the adult promote scarring upon spinal cord injury in mice.
source: For example, in the spinal cord, while neonatal microglia and astrocytes facilitate scarless repair, the same cells in the adult promote scarring upon spinal cord injury in mice (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dying cells release many factors, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) that activate signaling cascades in neighboring cells.
source: Dying cells release many factors, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) that activate signaling cascades in neighboring cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The level of ROS during homeostasis is regulated by metabolic processes and typically is increased following injury.
source: The level of ROS during homeostasis is regulated by metabolic processes and typically is increased following injury (Niethammer, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ROS can directly react with proteins that regulate proliferation, viability, quiescence, differentiation, and metabolism.
source: Furthermore, ROS can directly react with proteins that regulate proliferation, viability, quiescence, differentiation, and metabolism (Bigarella et al., 2014; Tan and Suda, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ROS are considered key signaling molecules that participate in the crosstalk between progenitor cell fate decisions and metabolic switches in a context- and cell type-dependent manner.
source: Thus, ROS are considered key signaling molecules that participate in the crosstalk between progenitor cell fate decisions and metabolic switches in a context- and cell type-dependent manner (Bigarella et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ROS signaling is implicated during inflammatory responses following an injury through the activation of microglia, which in turn can lead to more ROS production.
source: One significant mechanism by which ROS signaling is implicated during inflammatory responses following an injury is through the activation of microglia, which in turn can lead to more ROS production (Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: scRNA-seq analysis revealed the expected three distinct groups of cells: gliogenic-NEPs and astrocytes (Hopx+ clusters 2, 3, 6, 10), neurogenic-NEPs (Ascl1+ clusters 5, 8, 11), and GCP (Atoh1+ clusters 1, 4, 7, 12, 14).
source: The analysis revealed the expected three distinct groups of cells: gliogenic-NEPs and astrocytes (Hopx+ clusters 2, 3, 6, 10), neurogenic-NEPs (Ascl1+ clusters 5, 8, 11), and GCP (Atoh1+ clusters 1, 4, 7, 12, 14) that were present at each stage and in both conditions (Figure 1B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data and clustering analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Oligodendrocyte progenitors (cluster 15), microglia (clusters 17, 21), ependymal cells (clusters 13, 18, 19), and meninges (cluster 16) were detected in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: In addition, oligodendrocyte progenitors (cluster 15), microglia (clusters 17, 21), ependymal cells (clusters 13, 18, 19), and meninges (cluster 16) were detected (Figure 1B and D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 24 hr after injury at P1, 132 genes in gliogenic-NEP clusters were significantly upregulated in IR compared to 34 genes that were upregulated in nonIR P2 cells.
source: 24 hr after injury at P1, 132 genes in gliogenic-NEP clusters were significantly upregulated in IR compared to 34 genes that were upregulated in nonIR P2 cells (adjusted p-value≤0.05, Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The significantly increased genes in gliogenic-NEPs after injury included Cdkn1a, Phlda3, Ass1, and Bax, all of which have been implicated as increased in response to DNA damage and in ROS signaling, as well as in anti-apoptotic functions.
source: The significantly increased genes included Cdkn1a, Phlda3, Ass1, and Bax, all of which have been implicated as increased in response to DNA damage and in ROS signaling, as well as in anti-apoptotic functions (Figure 1G; Masgras et al., 2012; Bensellam et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data in Figure 1G and citations to prior literature.

claim: Many of the significant GO terms associated with the genes upregulated in gliogenic-NEPs with injury were related to response to irradiation, DNA damage, the p53 pathway, and ROS metabolic processes.
source: Indeed, many of the significant GO terms associated with the genes upregulated in gliogenic-NEPs with injury were related to response to irradiation, DNA damage, the p53 pathway, and ROS metabolic processes, whereas many of the significant GO terms associated with the genes upregulated in the nonIR cells at P2 were related to metabolic processes (p-value≤0.05, Figure 1H, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The transcriptional changes observed at P2 in gliogenic-NEPs were less pronounced at later time points (P3+5).
source: Interestingly, the transcriptional changes observed at P2 were less pronounced at later time points, where although some of the top differentially expressed genes at P2 were still significantly upregulated at P3+5 stages combined (e.g. Cdkn1a, Phlda3, Ass1, Bax), the increase in expression levels of these genes upon injury and/or the number of cells expressing them gradually declined after P2 in IR gliogenic-NEPs when compared to their nonIR counterparts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Injury induces major changes to the chromatin landscape of the NEPs (1168 differentially open regions, adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: Analysis of differentially open chromatin showed that injury induces major changes to the chromatin landscape of the NEPs (1168 differentially open regions, adjusted p-value<0.05, Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by bulk ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Cdkn1a and Phlda3 exhibited new accessible regions around their gene bodies compared to the nonIR P2 Nes-CFP+ cells.
source: Of interest, Cdkn1a and Phlda3, two genes stimulated by ROS and injury (Bensellam et al., 2019; Masgras et al., 2012) and that were upregulated in gliogenic-NEPs after irradiation (Figure 1F-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), exhibited new accessible regions around their gene bodies compared to the nonIR P2 Nes-CFP+ cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq tracks shown in Figure 1J and citations.

claim: Known motif analysis in the regions with increased accessibility upon injury showed enrichment for binding motifs of the JUN/AP1 transcriptional complex.
source: Known motif analysis in the regions with increased accessibility upon injury showed enrichment for binding motifs of the JUN/AP1 transcriptional complex (p-value = 10–14, % of target sequences with motif = 15%, Figure 1—source data 5), which is known to act in response to cellular stress and be activated by ROS.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: The DNA binding site for FOXO3, a transcription factor that regulates ROS levels, had increased chromatin accessibility.
source: In addition, the DNA binding site for FOXO3, a transcription factor that regulates ROS levels, had increased chromatin accessibility (p-value = 0.001, % of target sequences with motif = 22.41%) (Figure 1—source data 5; Filosto et al., 2003; Auten and Davis, 2009; Hagenbuchner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of ATAC-seq data and citations.

claim: A significant increase in ROS (cells present in the top 90% MitoSOX+ intensity) was observed specifically at P2 and not at P3 or P5 in IR pups compared to nonIR.
source: A significant increase in ROS (cells present in the top 90% MitoSOX+ intensity) was observed specifically at P2 (p=0.0005, n≥10) and not at P3 or P5 in IR pups compared to nonIR (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Quantification of mitochondrial mass with MitoTracker revealed a reduction only at P2 in IR pups.
source: Furthermore, quantification of mitochondrial mass with MitoTracker revealed a reduction only at P2 (p=0.0005, n≥10) in IR pups (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Quantification of TUNEL staining showed a large increase in cell death in the EGL of injured cerebella at P2, but not at P3 compared to the controls.
source: Additionally, quantification of TUNEL staining in midline sagittal sections of the cerebella showed a large increase in cell death in the EGL of injured cerebella at P2 (p=0.0040, n=4), but not at P3 compared to the controls (Figure 2D and E; see also Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Outside the EGL, there was a small increase in cell death after injury that was only significant at P3.
source: Outside the EGL, there was a small increase in cell death after injury that was only significant at P3 (p=0.0379, n≥3) (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A transient increase in ROS in the cerebellum 1 day after irradiation at P1 correlates with the timing of the major death of GCPs.
source: Thus, a transient increase in ROS in the cerebellum 1 day after irradiation at P1 correlates with the timing of the major death of GCPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between ROS increase and cell death shown in Figure 2.

claim: GFAP was first detected in rare astrocytes at P2 located in the WM below the lobules, with strong expression in all WM astrocytes at P5 and later stages (P8 and P12).
source: GFAP was first detected in rare astrocytes at P2 located in the WM below the lobules, with strong expression in all WM astrocytes at P5 and later stages (P8 and P12) (Figure 3A–D, observed in n=4 mice/stage).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GFAP expression in astrocytes in the developing IGL and in the glial processes of Bg that project through the molecular layer (ML) and EGL was not detectable until P5 and was much stronger at P8 and P12.
source: In contrast, GFAP expression in astrocytes in the developing IGL and in the glial processes of Bg that project through the molecular layer (ML) and EGL was not detectable until P5 and was much stronger at P8 and P12 (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: After injury at birth, GFAP expression was prematurely upregulated in the WM astrocytes below the lobules at P2 and in the remaining astrocytes at P5, including in the fibers of Bg that extend through the ML and EGL, compared to nonIR cerebella.
source: Interestingly, after injury at birth, GFAP expression was prematurely upregulated in the WM astrocytes below the lobules at P2 and in the remaining astrocytes at P5, including in the fibers of Bg that extend through the ML and EGL, compared to nonIR cerebella (Figure 3A–H, observed in n=4 mice/stage).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The density of IBA1+ microglia in the WM increased between P2 (235.1±18.3 cells/mm2) and P3 (344.3±53.1 cells/mm2) and then was maintained at P5 (350.4±40.2 cells/mm2).
source: We found that nearly all microglia were located in the WM of the cerebellum, and that the density of IBA1+ microglia in the WM increased between P2 (235.1±18.3 cells/mm2) and P3 (344.3±53.1 cells/mm2) and then was maintained at P5 (350.4±40.2 cells/mm2) (Figure 3I–K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of IBA1+ cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: After irradiation, the density of microglia in the injured EGL was significantly increased (~3-fold) at P2 but not at P3 or P5 compared to controls.
source: As expected, after irradiation, the density of microglia in the injured EGL was significantly increased (~3-fold) at P2 but not at P3 or P5 compared to controls (p=0.0331, n=4) (Figure 3L–N, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of IBA1+ cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: No difference in the microglial density in the WM was detected between conditions at both time points (P2 and P3).
source: No difference in the microglial density in the WM was detected between conditions at both time points (Figure 3I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of IBA1+ cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: mCAT protein is expressed throughout the cerebellum.
source: We confirmed that mCAT protein is expressed throughout the cerebellum using immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of cerebellar sections (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: MitoSOX flow cytometry revealed a significant decrease in ROS in the cerebella of mCAT mice 1 day after irradiation (P2) and not at P3 or P5 compared to control IR mice.
source: MitoSOX flow cytometry revealed a significant decrease in ROS in the cerebella of mCAT mice 1 day after irradiation (P2) (p=0.0163, n≥8) and not at P3 or P5 compared to control IR mice and no baseline decrease in ROS at any stage in nonIR mice (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mitochondrial mass, as measured by MitoTracker flow cytometry, was reduced at P2 in mCAT IR compared to nonIR mCAT pups, with no significant difference observed between mCAT and control IR mice.
source: Mitochondrial mass, as measured by MitoTracker flow cytometry, was reduced at P2 in mCAT IR compared to nonIR mCAT pups, with no significant difference observed between mCAT and control IR mice (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The level of cell death in the EGL and density of IBA1+ microglia in the EGL and elsewhere in the cerebellum were similar between mCAT and littermate control IR mice at P2 and P3.
source: The level of cell death in the EGL and density of IBA1+ microglia in the EGL and elsewhere in the cerebellum were similar between mCAT and littermate control IR mice at P2 and P3 (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and J).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and IBA1 staining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mCAT transgene counteracts the transient increase in cerebellar ROS following EGL injury but does not have a major effect on GCP death or the infiltration of microglia to the injured EGL.
source: Thus, the mCAT transgene counteracts the transient increase in cerebellar ROS following EGL injury but does have a major effect on GCP death or the infiltration of microglia to the injured EGL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The cross-sectional area of the medial cerebellum (vermis) of IR mCAT adult mice was significantly reduced compared to IR controls.
source: Strikingly, the cross-sectional area of the medial cerebellum (vermis) of IR mCAT adult mice was significantly reduced compared to IR controls (p=0.0040, n≥6) (Figure 4G–K).
evidence: This is supported by cerebellar area measurements shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The vermis sectional area of the IR mCAT cerebella was only significantly reduced at P30 compared to IR controls.
source: Analysis of cerebellar area across ages (P3, 5, 8, and 12) revealed that the vermis sectional area of the IR mCAT cerebella was only significantly reduced at P30 compared to IR controls; however, at P12, it was reduced in mCAT IR cerebella compared to mCAT nonIR mice, whereas it was not significantly different between control IR and control nonIR mice (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–N).
evidence: This is supported by cerebellar area measurements shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Cerebellar growth begins to be reduced at P12 in mCAT mice following injury.
source: These results indicate that cerebellar growth begins to be reduced at P12 in mCAT mice following injury.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cerebellar area data.

claim: A reduction in ROS at the time of cell death in the EGL leads to a diminution of cerebellar recovery.
source: Thus, a reduction in ROS at the time of cell death in the EGL leads to a diminution of cerebellar recovery.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mCAT mouse data.

claim: The thickness of the EGL in IR mice of both genotypes was similarly reduced compared to nonIR mice at P5.
source: Interestingly, we found that although the thickness of the EGL in IR mice of both genotypes was similarly reduced compared to nonIR mice at P5 (p=0.0041 control and p=0.0005 mCAT; n≥4) by P8, the control EGL was a similar thickness to the control nonIR, whereas the thickness of the mCAT IR EGL was significantly reduced compared to mCAT nonIR mice (p=0.035, n=4) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by EGL thickness measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: By P8, the control EGL was a similar thickness to the control nonIR, whereas the thickness of the mCAT IR EGL was significantly reduced compared to mCAT nonIR mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that although the thickness of the EGL in IR mice of both genotypes was similarly reduced compared to nonIR mice at P5 (p=0.0041 control and p=0.0005 mCAT; n≥4) by P8, the control EGL was a similar thickness to the control nonIR, whereas the thickness of the mCAT IR EGL was significantly reduced compared to mCAT nonIR mice (p=0.035, n=4) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by EGL thickness measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The density of CFP+ cells in the EGL (mainly BgL-derived NEPs) was significantly decreased in mCAT IR mice compared to control IR mice at P5 but not P3.
source: Strikingly, the density of CFP+ cells in the EGL (mainly BgL-derived NEPs) was significantly decreased in mCAT IR mice compared to control IR mice at P5 (p=0.0002, n=4) but not P3 (Figure 5C–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by CFP+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The density of NEPs (CFP+ or SOX2+ cells) in the BgL was significantly decreased at P5 in mCAT IR cerebella compared to controls but not at other stages.
source: Furthermore, the density of NEPs (CFP+ or SOX2+ cells) in the BgL was significantly decreased at P5 in mCAT IR cerebella compared to controls (p=0.0010, n≥5) but not at other stages (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by NEP density measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: BgL-NEPs have a blunted response to EGL injury and therefore do not fully expand and contribute to the replenishment of GCPs in the EGL after irradiation in mCAT mice.
source: These results indicate that BgL-NEPs have a blunted response to EGL injury and therefore do not fully expand and contribute to the replenishment of GCPs in the EGL after irradiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced NEP density and EGL replenishment in mCAT mice.

claim: Control IR mice had a similar number of IBA1+ cells in the WM as nonIR mice of both genotypes at P5.
source: Interestingly, whereas control IR mice had a similar number of IBA1+ cells in the WM as nonIR mice of both genotypes at P5, the mCAT IR mice had a lower density of microglia/macrophages in the WM compared to control IR mice at P5 (p=0.0012, n≥3) (Figure 6A–D and F), but no significant changes were observed at P8 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by IBA1+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mCAT IR mice had a lower density of microglia/macrophages in the WM compared to control IR mice at P5.
source: Interestingly, whereas control IR mice had a similar number of IBA1+ cells in the WM as nonIR mice of both genotypes at P5, the mCAT IR mice had a lower density of microglia/macrophages in the WM compared to control IR mice at P5 (p=0.0012, n≥3) (Figure 6A–D and F), but no significant changes were observed at P8 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by IBA1+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: IBA1+ cells were significantly decreased in the cerebellum of PLX-treated mice at P5 compared to their controls, both nonIR and IR.
source: As expected, IBA1+ cells were significantly decreased in the cerebellum of PLX-treated mice at P5 compared to their controls, both nonIR and IR (p=0.0015 and p=0.0059, n=3 and n=5, respectively) (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by IBA1+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The thickness of the EGL was not significantly altered at P5 in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls.
source: The thickness of the EGL was not significantly altered at P5 in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by EGL thickness measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The density of Nes-CFP+ cells in the EGL was significantly decreased in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls at P5.
source: Interestingly, similar to mCAT mice, the density of Nes-CFP+ cells in the EGL was significantly decreased in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls at P5 (p=0.0008, n=5) (Figure 6I–M).
evidence: This is supported by CFP+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The density of SOX2+ cells in the BgL was unchanged in the PLX-treated and control mice, whether irradiated or not.
source: In contrast, the density of SOX2+ cells in the BgL, corresponding to the gliogenic BgL-NEPs, was unchanged in the PLX-treated and control mice, whether irradiated or not, suggesting that the decrease in expansion of BgL-NEPs caused by ROS is not mediated by microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by SOX2+ cell density measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The cerebellar vermis section area was not decreased in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls at P30.
source: When mice were treated with PLX from P0 to P8 and allowed to age to P30, we found the cerebellar vermis section area was not decreased in PLX-treated IR mice compared to IR controls (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is supported by cerebellar area measurements shown in Figure 6N.

claim: Reducing the density of IBA1+ microglia/macrophages in neonatal mice reduces the recruitment of Nes-CFP+ cells to the EGL at P5 but does not have a long-term significant impact on regeneration of the cerebellum.
source: Thus, reducing the density of IBA1+ microglia/macrophages in neonatal mice reduces the recruitment of Nes-CFP+ cells to the EGL at P5 but does not have a long-term significant impact on regeneration of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PLX treatment data.

claim: A transient increase in ROS signaling after cerebellar injury to the EGL is critical for adaptive reprogramming and full recovery of cerebellar growth.
source: We demonstrate that a transient increase in ROS signaling after cerebellar injury to the EGL is critical for adaptive reprogramming and full recovery of cerebellar growth.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ROS likely acts as an alarm signal shortly after injury.
source: ROS likely acts as an alarm signal shortly after injury.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing and effects of ROS increase.

claim: By reducing mitochondrial ROS levels across all cell types at P2 using an mCAT transgene, we uncovered that ROS is required for several steps of adaptive reprogramming of BgL-NEPs.
source: By reducing mitochondrial ROS levels across all cell types at P2 using an mCAT transgene, we uncovered that ROS is required for several steps of adaptive reprogramming of BgL-NEPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mCAT mouse experiments.

claim: Microglia are reduced in injured mCAT pups.
source: In addition, we found that microglia are reduced in injured mCAT pups, which is consistent with prior evidence that ROS can trigger immune cell recruitment in other systems (Kim et al., 2010; Mehl et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by IBA1+ cell density measurements in Figure 6 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Temporary depletion of microglia caused a reduction in the number of NEPs that migrate into the EGL at P5 following injury at P1, but no long-term reduction of cerebellar size.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PLX treatment experiments.

claim: The ability of BgL-NEPs to respond to GCP death via upregulating ROS signaling and impaired regeneration upon reduction of ROS levels shows that ROS signaling is involved in triggering adaptive reprogramming upon injury.
source: The ability of BgL-NEPs to respond to GCP death via upregulating ROS signaling and impaired regeneration upon reduction of ROS levels shows that ROS signaling is involved in triggering adaptive reprogramming upon injury.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the scRNA-seq and mCAT mouse data.

claim: Neonatal astrocytes respond to injury differently than in the adult where GFAP upregulation is observed immediately after injury.
source: These results suggest that the neonatal astrocytes respond to injury differently than in the adult where GFAP upregulation is observed immediately after injury (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014), since Bg and astrocytes in the lobules have a delayed response to injury with GFAP not being upregulated for several days.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GFAP expression data and comparison to adult brain injury literature.

claim: Neonatal microglia are transcriptionally distinct from adult microglia.
source: Furthermore, at birth, the microglia have not fully expanded in number in the cerebellum, and previous scRNA-seq showed that the neonatal and adult microglia are transcriptionally distinct (Hammond et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neonatal microglia may be anti-inflammatory and pro-regenerative upon injury in neonates, in contrast to adult microglia.
source: Perhaps neonatal microglia are anti-inflammatory and pro-regenerative upon injury in neonates, in contrast to adult microglia, where upon traumatic brain injury, they can inhibit regeneration (Donat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the differences between neonatal and adult microglia and citation to adult brain injury literature.

claim: The differences in glial responses to injury in the neonatal cerebellum and adult brain likely contribute to the permissiveness of the neonatal cerebellum to regeneration.
source: Collectively, the differences in glial responses to injury in the neonatal cerebellum and adult brain likely contribute to the permissiveness of the neonatal cerebellum to regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in glial responses.

claim: In mCAT neonatal cerebella, the percentage of MitoSOX high cells was comparable to control mice under nonIR conditions.
source: However, in mCAT neonatal cerebella, we found that the percentage of MitoSOX high cells was comparable to control mice under nonIR conditions.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: 1 day after irradiation at P1 when the percentage of MitoSOX high cells increases in control IR mice, the mCAT transgene reduces the percentage of MitoSOX high cells, such that it remains at the baseline nonIR mCAT level.

evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Human CAT expression in mitochondria in the mCAT model inhibits the injury-induced increase in ROS levels without affecting the homeostatic production of superoxide.
source: Therefore, human CAT expression in mitochondria in this model inhibits the injury-induced increase in ROS levels without affecting the homeostatic production of superoxide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data showing ROS levels in mCAT mice.

claim: Microglia/macrophages are involved in the regeneration of the EGL following irradiation.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PLX treatment experiments.

claim: Neonatal microglia are involved in the adaptive reprogramming of NEPs to GCPs by promoting their replenishment of GCPs in the EGL.

evidence: This is an inference based on the PLX treatment data showing reduced NEP recruitment to the EGL.

claim: ROS signaling is a key stimulator of adaptive reprogramming of NEPs.
source: Collectively, we have delineated the spatiotemporal cellular changes in the cerebellar glial microenvironment upon ablation of GCPs at birth and highlight ROS signaling as a key stimulator of adaptive reprogramming of NEPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.
